en: The Method for the Practice of the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja according to the Yoga of the Vajraśekhara Sūtra,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi of South India during the Tang Dynasty.
Now, relying upon the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*,
I shall expound the essential Dharma of the Vajrapadma.
First, one must enter the consecration samaya-maṇḍala.
One should generate the great bodhicitta,
benefit all beings by relinquishing body, life, and wealth,
and apply oneself with courageous diligence in accordance with mindfulness.
One who possesses compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity without interruption—
only such a person should practice these methods,
including the drawing of the maṇḍala and its images.
As has been explained at length elsewhere:
whenever one enters a vihāra with the desire to practice mindfulness,
one should first touch the five limbs to the ground.
I prostrate to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja, the presiding deity. Next,
I prostrate to the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi of the north,
and so forth, up to the Tathāgatas Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, and Vairocana.
All of them, according to the ritual, prostrated with utmost sincerity and respect;
kneeling on both knees,
they joined their palms in the lotus gesture.
I repent for all transgressions of the three karmas.
Having been mired in the ocean of birth and death for immeasurable kalpas,
I now, with a purified mind, disclose and repent my faults.
Just as all Buddhas have performed confession, so do I now likewise vow that I and all sentient beings shall all be completely purified.

Recite this mantra: Oṃ sarvabhāvaśuddhaḥ sarvadharmāḥ sarvabhāvaśuddho ’haṃ. Next, one should rejoice in the merit and wisdom accumulated by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, present, and future.
The roots of goodness accumulated by the Buddhas of the past, present, and future, as well as by bodhisattvas and sentient beings—
having joined one’s palms, one should rejoice in them all; next,
one should place the right knee on the ground and, with palms hollowed and joined, place them upon the crown of the head.
Visualize paying homage to the feet of all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Bodhisattvas.
Recite the secret mantra:
Oṃ padma vande. Having thus paid homage to all the Buddhas, [proceed].
Sitting upon the seat in the mudrā, one enters meditative absorption and contemplates.
One visualizes immeasurable Tathāgatas pervading the entire Dharma-realm,
with the practitioner’s own body present within all those assemblies.
Thereafter, perform the binding of the secret samaya:
join the tips of the six fingers together,
and slightly bend the index and middle fingers to press down upon the upper ridges of the ring and little fingers.
Pressing the dhyāna and wisdom [mudrās] with force as described below,
place them upon the crown of the head.
The mantra is:
Oṃ tathāgatodbhavāya svāhā. Next, bind the mudrā of the Lotus Family Samaya Dhāraṇī:
join the two hands in the lotus-anjali gesture.
The head of the dhyāna-wisdom (dhyāna-prajñā) almsbowl rests against the head of the wisdom-almsgiving (prajñā-dāna) bowl.
The heads of these six bowls are spaced one inch apart from one another.
They are placed upon the right ear.
Recite the mantra:
Oṃ baddhamudrāya svāhā. Next, bind the Vajrakula-samaya-dhāraṇī and its mudrā.
Immediately take the wisdom of dāna and the wisdom of dhyāna-prajñā;
turning them over and over, hook them together with one another.
First, form the mudrā at the center of the heart.
Place the wondrous words in the left ear;
advance the secret words three times;
when the speech is finished, scatter the Cakravartin from the crown of the head.
The mantra is:
Oṃ vajra-nābhāya svāhā. Next, perform the binding of the Vajra-body protection dhāraṇī and its mudrā.
Then, with the fingers of the *śīla* (vow) hand and the *dāna* (generosity) hand interlaced within,
raise the two fingers of the *kṣānti* (patience) and *praṇidhāna* (vow) hands like banners;
bend the *vīrya* (effort) and *bala* (power) fingers back against the backs of the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhāna* fingers.
The back [of the hands] is bent three finger-widths into a hook-like shape;
the two fingers of wisdom (tarjanī) and dhyāna (madhyamā) are held upright at the heart.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ vajrāgni-pratāpana svāhā. Next, bind the mudrā and recite the Vajrajvālā-bhūmī-dhāraṇī.
One enters the perfection of patience through the perfection of aspiration;
one enters the perfection of wisdom through the perfection of ethical discipline;
and by means of the perfection of aspiration.
From the back, it enters between the *kṣānti-pāramitā* and the *upāya-pāramitā*.
Through skillful means, it enters between the *dāna-pāramitā* and the *śīla-pāramitā*.
The *dāna*, *prajñā*, *vīrya*, *bala*, *dhyāna*, and *jñāna* each butt their heads against one another.
Cover it facing downward.
With the *dhyāna* and *prajñā* fingers planted on the ground like the posture of driving in a stake,
recite the mantra three times while visualizing [the hand] as a single-pronged vajra with flaming fire.
Piercing through to the adamantine limit,
recite the mantra:
Oṃ kili kili vajra vajriṇi bhūr bhuvaḥ svāhā | phaṭ | This is the mantra and mudrā for the adamantine fire-city, the soaring flame, the lightning, and the boundary of the enclosure.
Perform the earth-seal as before;
open wide the *citta* and *prajñā* fingers and rotate them clockwise through the eight directions.
Recite the mantra as follows:
Oṃ sara sara vajraprakāra hūṃ phaṭ. This mantra and mudrā for the boundary of the vajra-flame net is performed using the same earth-mudrā as before.
Open wide and establish the wisdom of direct Zen;
cover it from above, moving it back and forth three times,
while visualizing a net of vajra-flame fire.
Extending upward to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the mantra is:
Oṃ viśvapralokita-vajra-bhañjara hūṃ phaṭ. Next, one forms the mudrā of the Vajra Flame Fire Boundary (*vajrajvālāgnimaṇḍala*).
The Samādhi and Prajñā [fingers] touch each other at their sides;
the Dhyāna and Jñāna [fingers] are held upright with a distance of three cun between them,
curling to the right at the tips.
Visualize the walls and the net, and recite the secret mantra:
Oṃ asamañgini svāhā. Once this realm has been established, [proceed].
The six classes of Māras and all the Vināyakas, struck with terror,
fled in all directions, finding no place to hide.
Next, one should bind the seal of Avalokiteśvara’s precious chariot.
With the two hands, interlace them with the palms facing upward;
with the *jñāna* and *dhyāna* fingers, beckon the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhi* fingers inward,
and flick them three times.
While reciting the mantra, one should visualize the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) arriving according to one’s wish;
one should continuously contemplate within the secret mind that the mind is an illusory, floating bubble.
The secret mantra is as follows:
Oṃ tura tura hūṃ. Next, form the mudrā of the eight great lotuses:
interlace the two hands, and join the tips of the middle fingers, the thumbs, and the heads of the ring fingers together.
Dhyāna, praṇidhāna, jñāna, and kṣānti each support one another.
One should visualize the three secret mantras placed upon a chariot atop a white eight-petaled lotus within the space of one cubit.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ khaṃ-ma-ra-svā-hā. Next, bind the yoga-secret-samaya-mudrā:
with both hands, form a firm fist;
join the thumbs and ring fingers respectively, and extend them upright.
Awaken [the deity] with the mudrā, reciting the mantra:
Oṃ vajrapadma-samayas-tvaṃ. Next, bind the Samaya-mudrā of the Bliss, Joy, and Delight of All Tathāgatas.
The ten fingers are firmly bound; the thumbs and ring fingers are joined at their centers.
The thumbs and little fingers are joined together and held upright.
The mantra is recited as follows:
Oṃ samayas tvam saraḥ tathāgata-satvaṃ. Next, bind the heart-gate and enter the syllable *vajrajñāna*.
Visualize it above the two breasts.
With the right hand at *tara* and the left at *ṭa*,
like the door-panels of a palace,
this is the supreme Vajra-bond.
The three karmas arise simultaneously.
Pointing to the mind, one opens the two characters.
The mantra says:
The seeds perfumed since beginningless time And the accumulated afflictions—
Now, by means of the mudrā for summoning transgressions, I gather them in order to shatter them;
With the ten perfections as firm bonds, I extend the fingers of patience and aspiration like needles.
The advancing force is bent like a hook; with the mind, one visualizes the summoning of all sins.
One should visualize those various sinful forms—hair standing erect, naked and black in shape—with their hands inverted and piercing the heart.
Having touched [the object], one recites the secret mantra.
Because it is associated with the three karmas, it can summon all accumulated sins.
Having recited this invocation, one then performs the rite of destruction.
The secret mantra is as follows:
Having summoned [the deity] into the palms, one then performs the method of crushing:
cross the two hands in front, recite *māṃ bandha*,
extend both the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhāna* fingers straight, and [place] the syllable *taraṭa*.
Visualize yourself as a vajra; clashing it together like a mountain being shattered, with wrathful hooks and fierce forms, you can exhaust all evil destinies.
Having recited [the mantra], clap with the hands of patience and aspiration twenty-one times, as appropriate for the occasion.
With universal compassion, one gathers all;
summoning them in, one strikes away all defilements and crushes all māras.
All are thus eliminated and purified like the full moon; one should contemplate the eight-petaled lotus.
Visualize [the deity] within the heart; join the two elbows with the palms facing upward and held erect like a precious lotus, with the ten fingers slightly separated.
Slightly bending [the fingers], perform the movement of the eight petals while reciting the secret mantra.
By means of this gateway of correspondence, through the skillful means of the Buddhas of the past,
the sins accumulated by the three karmas and immeasurable,
most heavy obstructions are utterly destroyed, like fire consuming dry grass.
Sentient beings are perpetually deluded and do not understand this principle;
therefore, out of the Tathāgata’s great compassion, he has opened this secret and wondrous gate.
Next, one should perform the mudrā of entry.
The syllable Jñāna (the Tathāgata) is within;
with the two hands firmly bound,
the dhyāna and jñāna fingers enter into the center.
With the two powers of progress,
they support one another like the shape of a ring;
contemplate the eight-petaled lotus in front.
Upon it is placed the syllable *sa*;
because it is adorned with two dots (*bindu*),
this wondrous syllable is able to summon even the malevolent.
The color is white like jade or snow,
radiating a thousand beams of light;
contemplate this with the power of progress.
Rolling the syllables within the mind to settle it,
employ the three karmas in unison.
Recite this secret mantra as follows:
Oṃ vajravesāya hūṃ. Visualize [the syllable] entering the heart;
visualize the syllable as exceedingly radiant.
This is the essence of the dharmadhātu.
The practitioner should contemplate thus;
before long they will realize purity,
for phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.
The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time,
with their vajra body, speech, and mind,
all employ sublime skillful means.
Holding the vajra-fist,
one thus closes the gate of the heart;
through the syllable JÑĀ, firmness is attained.
Then, bending the forefinger,
one supports it against the back of the ring finger;
having touched the chest with the seal, [one recites the mantra].
Then recite this sublime mantra:
Oṃ vajramuṣṭi vaṃ. Next, perform the seal for closing the heart-door of all Buddhas’ vajras.
Then, with the eight fingers interlaced,
first starting from the right and turning to the left,
one moves back and forth three times to turn the door panel.
Visualize closing the gates of the mind with these three secret mantras. The mantra is:
Oṃ padma dūṣi. Next is the mudrā for binding, expelling, and delimiting the boundary.
Immediately place both palms together at the heart;
join the right hand over the left with fingers interlaced externally,
and raise the two thumbs (the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhāna* fingers) like a banner.
Next, using the power of exertion, hook the square of the precepts;
join the tips of the fingers of dhyāna, prajñā, and dāna.
The secret mantra is as follows:
Oṃ amṛtodbhava hūṃ phaṭ. This dharma is the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara manifested as Hayagrīva Vidyārāja.
Having empowered the practitioner so that they may swiftly attain Buddhahood,
perform this boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) by circling three times to the left to expel what is unwholesome,
and then circling three times to the right to establish the boundary at whatever distance one desires.
Next, having performed the empowerment-binding (*adhiṣṭhāna-bandha*), visualize the true form by arranging the syllables.
As for the seal placed there, it is clearly the syllable *Hrīḥ*;
these syllables must all appear together within the lunar disk (*candramaṇḍala*).
Then, emit the light from the white tuft of hair, and cause it to gradually withdraw;
join the two palms at the heart, interlace the ten fingers with the left over the right,
extend the thumbs straight upward, and seal the crown and the forehead.
First, from the right eye, [place the syllables] upon the two shoulders, the heart, the navel, and the knees, proceeding to the left;
then recite the secret mantra *Oṃ aruli svāhā* while forming this mudrā to arrange the syllables upon the body.
One’s own body shall then become like the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion,
endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, a body of purple-gold hue, and a perfect radiance, empowered by the Tathāgatas.
Having formed this mental image, one uses the hand-seal to touch the crown of the head and arrange the syllable Oṃ; then,
touching the forehead, one arranges the syllable A.
Touch the eyes with the syllable *Bhruṃ*.
Then, using each syllable in successive order,
extend the placement down to both feet.
Visualize the syllable Oṃ placed upon the head; white in color like the moon, it emits immeasurable light.
It eliminates all obstacles, making one identical to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and touches the crown of this person’s head.
The letter A is placed upon the forehead; its color is entirely golden, illuminating all ignorance and darkness, and capable of generating the light of profound wisdom.
The letter RU is placed above the two eyes; its color is like deep blue lapis lazuli.
It can manifest all forms and appearances; gradually possessing the power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, one should visualize it resting upon both shoulders.
Its color is like pure white silk because the mind is pure; thus, one will swiftly reach the path to Bodhi.
*Svāhā* is placed at the navel for peace;
one should constantly visualize this syllable as being red in color, and one will swiftly attain the turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
*Ha* is placed upon the two feet; its color is like that of the full moon.
When the practitioner forms this visualization, they will swiftly attain parinirvāṇa.
Thus, by contemplating the form of one’s own root-syllable, one accomplishes the supreme dharma-gate of great compassion.
Furthermore, it is the true form of one’s respective tutelary deity; it can extinguish all sins and bring about auspiciousness.
Like a vajra, a solid mass of firmness—this is called the supreme dharma of great compassion.
If one constantly practices such a dharma, know that this person will swiftly attain *siddhi*.
(Recite three times to purify the seal.)
Visualize within your own mind the Great Compassionate One, Avalokiteśvara.

From his thousand eyes and mouth, the wondrous syllables of the Great Compassionate One’s speech emerge, emitting light of five colors that enters the practitioner’s mouth and is arranged clockwise within the moon disc of one’s own heart; then, recite the mantra of the Honored One once.
Using the ring finger of the right hand, grasp one bead;
when it has passed through the circle, begin again.
Neither too hurried nor too slow, and likewise not in a loud voice.
One must clearly pronounce the syllables so that they are heard by oneself, while simultaneously visualizing the principal deity being contemplated and the syllables arrayed upon one's body;
during a single moment of thought, all of these must be perceived at once.
One must not allow any deficiency that would cause the mind to become distracted.
If one becomes weary from mental visualization,
one should recite according to one's capacity, fixing the limit at a constant number such as one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, up to seven hundred or one thousand.
If there are matters requiring one's presence, one must still perform the recitation without omission or deficiency.
If one seeks liberation and transcendence from birth and death,
performing the contemplative practice of samādhi-yoga, there is no fixed limit to the number of recitations.
The practitioner should visualize his own mind as being like a full moon,
serene, pure, and clearly distinct both internally and externally.
He should place the syllable Oṃ within the heart of the moon and [recite] Aruli Svāhā.
From the beginning, arrange them in clockwise order around the perimeter of the wheel;
contemplate each syllable with keen attention,
ensuring that its meaning corresponds with the mind.
One must not err.
The syllable *Oṃ* signifies the meaning of continuous flow;
it also signifies the meaning of neither arising nor ceasing.
Among all phenomena, it is the supreme meaning.
The syllable A signifies non-arising;
it is also the wisdom of quiescence within the teachings of all Tathāgatas.
The syllable *ru* signifies that all phenomena have no sense of activity,
nor do they possess the sense of arising or abiding.
The syllable *la* signifies the peerless awakening of all Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, it has no meaning of acceptance or rejection.
The syllable *svā* signifies that all Tathāgatas are peerless and beyond verbal expression.
The syllable *ha* signifies causelessness and quiescence.
Nor is there the meaning of abiding in nirvāṇa.
All the meanings of the words as explained above are,
in fact, the meaning of words that have nothing to be expressed.
Having realized that there are no words or letters,
one then contemplates that, in terms of their true meaning and principle, there is actually nothing to be said;
it revolves in cycles without beginning or end, beyond description and enumeration.
Nor is it ever interrupted.
That which is uninterrupted is precisely the meaning of "continuous flow," being neither born nor extinguished.
Because it is neither born nor extinguished, there is no conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*).
Because there is no activity, there is no contradiction;
because there is no contradiction, there is neither arising nor abiding;
and because there is neither arising nor abiding, there is no equal enlightenment.
That which is without grasping or rejecting is itself equanimity.
Being beyond verbal expression,
it is the silence of causelessness, precisely because it is the speech of equanimity.
Non-abiding nirvana is the nirvana of non-abiding that is quiescent due to the absence of causes;
it is precisely neither arising nor ceasing.
This is the most supreme dharma-gate of all Tathāgatas,
called the Samādhi Recitation.
Next, bind the Samādhi Mudrā.
The two hands are held with palms facing upward and crossed;
the thumbs are turned inward and held upright,
while the ring fingers and little fingers grasp the tips of the thumbs.
Placing [the hands] upon the crossed legs,
the practitioner next cultivates the āśvāsapraśvāsa-samādhi (concentration on inhalation and exhalation),
sitting upright with the body straightened.
The body remains motionless;
the tongue is pressed against the upper palate;
and the inhalation and exhalation of breath are stilled.
Cause it to become subtle;
contemplate all phenomena with discernment as being entirely derived from one's own mind.
All afflictions are like flames and like illusions;
they possess no reality.
Having made this contemplation,
I pray only that all Buddhas will show me the path to be traversed.
Recite this mantra:
Oṃ samayapadmame hṛiḥ. At the time of sitting upright, each [syllable] should be clearly understood.
He beheld in the void of space immeasurable Buddhas,
who simultaneously snapped their fingers.
The vigilant practitioner addressed him, saying:
"Excellent! You are able to perform such a practice."
Within your visualization,
the syllable Aḥ that is arrayed in your heart is crystal clear and translucent.
Recite this mantra:
"One should contemplate that the mind is to be seen as perfectly full like the pure moon.
Furthermore, one should reflect: "From what does this mind arise?"
The seeds of the habitual tendencies of affliction—both good and evil—arise from the mind;
the mind is the ālayavijñāna. When it is cultivated for purity, it serves as the cause [of awakening];
yet, when obscured by adventitious defilements, it cannot achieve bodhi.
Then, recite this mantra: Oṃ bodhicittam utpādayāmi. Reciting this, contemplate the mind and cause it to become utterly clear and pure.
Just as there is no obstruction within the great expanse of space,
one should likewise visualize a single lotus flower within the heart.
This causes the moon-disc of the mind to become perfectly full and increasingly luminous,
manifesting a firm abiding in bodhicitta.
Then, he bestowed the heart-mantra.
Oṃ tiṣṭha vajra-padma. Visualize the lotus and the moon disk, gradually extending them throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Its measure is equal to space and is without obstruction;
this is the gate of the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*).
Within your pure lunar disc—
Contemplate the five wisdom-vajras as pervading the entire dharmadhātu,
becoming a single great vajra.
One should know that one's own body is the Vajradhātu.
The mantra says:
Recite this mantra: Oṃ sphara vajra padma.
Visualize that immeasurable light rays issue forth from within the lotus.
Immeasurable light radiates forth to immeasurable worlds;
each world is adorned with exquisite jewels,
and in every one dwells the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja.
Surrounded before and behind by the assembly of noble ones,
one realizes one's own mind and immediately attains purity.
One should know that one's own body has likewise become that Buddha,
fully endowed with all the marks of excellence.
Thereupon, while in meditative concentration,
he prostrated to all the Buddhas everywhere,
praying that they would grant their empowerment so that his resolve may be firm and steadfast.
Then he spoke the Vajra-Mind Mantra, saying:
Oṃ saṃhara-patma. Upon reciting this mantra, one immediately becomes endowed with the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñā-jñāna) and attains equal and perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
Next, perform the secret mudrā of empowerment:
interlace the six fingers of the thumbs and ring fingers externally;
extend the index and middle fingers so they rest like a lotus.
Visualize the union of meditative concentration and wisdom as a banner,
sealing the heart, forehead, throat,
and crown. The mantra is:
Oṃ vajradharma hṛīḥ. Visualize that all the Tathāgatas of space hold the jewel of space and sprinkle it upon my crown;
the vajra of union is formed by the blending of meditative concentration and wisdom.
The power of progress, meditation, and wisdom take the form of jewels;
having empowered the forehead with this seal,
there immediately appears a crown of the five Buddhas upon the head.
The secret mantra is:
Oṃ padmaratnābhiṣiñca sarvamaṃ hiriṭṭha. Next, form the mudrā of the lotus garland.
As before, place the two hands at the heart;
join the *dhyāna* and *prajñā* fingers and bend them into the palms;
form fists with the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhāna* fingers, each representing one of the six perfections.
Like a garland of flowers being slowly lowered, the mantra is:
Oṃ padmaratnamale muṃ. Next, bind the seal of the armor of universal loving-kindness.
The two wisdoms should certainly be held in the mind; with the power of progress, they intersect from the side,
visualizing the syllable Oṃ on the face of progress and the syllable Kṣa on the face of power,
emitting green light.
The light shines on without ceasing,
like drawing out lotus fibers.
Once the mind is settled within it, remain there.
Having bound the garland with the Wisdom Fist behind the forehead,
one then extends the Forearm of Progression downward in front.
Oṃ, *ciṇa*— twice, they are entwined around one another.
The green light does not cease, like armor fastened;
it extends from the heart and back, level with the waist, up to the two knees,
and across the chest, back, throat, neck, crown of the head, and the area behind the forehead.
Each advancing power circles three times;
with palms opened and lowered before one like celestial raiment,
one is thus able to universally protect all sentient beings.
Nothing can destroy it, not even all the celestial Māras.
The secret mantra is:
Oṃ apāya-padmaka-vajri-mandala-kṣe ḍaṃ hūṃ haṃ. Next, perform the seal of the Tathāgata’s Joy.
The two wings of concentration and wisdom are joined at the heart;
the two fingers of vigor and power are crossed externally;
the two fingers of meditation and wisdom are held upright at the heart.
Clapping the hands three times, one invokes all the noble ones.
The mantra is:
Oṃ padmadṛśya hoḥ. One should [enter] the samādhi of the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna).
Visualize before one's body an immeasurable ocean of milk,
from which arises a great king of lotuses.
The stem is made of vajra and its circumference measures the entire dharma-realm.
Above it is a jeweled pavilion containing a lion throne;
within a full moon, a wondrous white lotus appears.
One visualizes the syllable HRĪḤ within the ocean,
which transforms into a blossoming lotus;
this flower further transforms into the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja.
Countless bodhisattvas surrounded him from before and behind,
forming a retinue that had all gathered for this assembly.
Next, he bound the seal of the Bodhisattva Vajrarāja for summoning all the sages.
The two wings of concentration and wisdom form vajra-fists;
the right hand, like a hook, is extended with only the third finger bent.
The mantra is as follows:
Having recited this mantra— Oṃ padma-añkuśa hūṃ jaḥ— three times,
one should immediately summon [the deity] three times with the gesture of the supreme stride (pradāna-pada).
The *dharmakāya* bodhisattvas fill the void;
at the mere thought of them, they arrive from the ten directions simultaneously.
Next, bind the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the Vajra Lasso.
Introduce the honored body into the essence of wisdom.
Interlace the hands externally for the six perfections of patience and aspiration;
join the tips of the two fingers of meditation and diligence together.
Recite this mantra:
Oṃ padma-amogha-pāśa hūṃ. Then, visualize that the Dharma-body of the Bodhisattva enters the painted image, whereby it becomes the Dharma-body itself.
Next, bind the Vajra Hook-Chain mudrā;
it causes the deity to remain firmly established.
The signs of dhyāna, vīrya, bala, and jñāna are joined together like hooks.
This is called the Vajra-Śamana-mudrā. The mantra is:
Oṃ padma saṃpuṭa hūṃ. Having recited this dharma, [one should perform the rite].
The noble one’s own empowerment remains undispersed.
Next, form the mudrā of the sublime vajra bell.
Having formed this mudrā:
It causes all the noble ones to rejoice.
The dhyāna and wisdom fingers are bent into the vajra-bond;
the index and middle fingers are bent and joined like a ring.
This is called the Vajra-Ānanda-mudrā. The mantra is:
Oṃ padma-vaiśākha hoḥ. By means of this mantra and mudrā,
All Buddhas, Bodhisattvas,
and original holy ones will all be filled with joy.
Next, perform the mudrā and recite the mantra for the *argha* water.
Place both palms at the heart; join the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhāna* fingers (the ring and little fingers) to represent the six *pāramitās*;
then extend the *vīrya* and *bala* fingers (the index and middle fingers) upward and straight.
Curling the thumbs and ring fingers into the *jñāna-muṣṭi* mudrā, recite the mantra:
Oṃ dīpti-re buddha-vāk. With this, make offerings to all the Tathāgatas and Vajras.
By pouring the nectar upon the crowns of the heads of all sentient beings,
immeasurable karmic obstructions are extinguished;
this is due to this offering of argha water.
Bathing the stainless bodies of all the noble assembly,
the merit of this is immeasurable;
one shall thereby attain the stage of the Dharma-Cloud of Empowerment.
Next, perform the binding of the hundred-syllable mantra and mudrā of all Tathāgatas:
Oṃ vajrasattva samayam anupālaya vajrasattva-tvenopatiṣṭha.
Nṛtya-maṇḍapa-sudṛśya-maṇḍapa-anurāga-sudṛśya-maṇḍapa-svapna-sudṛśya-maṇḍapa-sarva-siddhi-maṇḍala-ācāra-sarva-karma-sucarita.
Camṛte śleṣmāyoge kuru hūṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ bhagavan sarvatathāgatapadma-maṃ mañcamuñca padme pāpamahe samayasattva āḥ. By this mahā...
By virtue of the empowerment of the hundred-syllable mantra,
even those who have committed the five crimes of immediate retribution or slandered the Vaipulya sutras of all the Buddhas—
such offenses as these shall all be completely extinguished.
Because the deity abides firmly within one's own body,
one swiftly attains the rank of Vajrasattva,
as well as the ranks of the Bodhisattvas and the Buddhas.
Next, bind the Vajralāsyā mudrā for the four inner offerings: join the wisdom and means [fingers] of the vajra fists.
Hold the two thumbs at the heart and extend them upward;
all playful movements gradually ascend in a wheel.
This mudrā of scattering upon the crown of the head accords with the sacred intent;
by performing this offering,
all Tathāgatas [are honored].
The offering of wisdom:
by means of this, the Buddhas engage in their playful pastimes.
The mantra is:
Oṃ padma-rāśe huḥ. Next, form the vajra-flower-garland mudrā;
without altering the previous mudrā, hold it out in front.
Visualize holding a precious garland to adorn the head.
The mantra is: Oṃ padmamālā-tṛtā. Through this mudrā and mantra, perform the offering.
One shall then obtain the position of the Dharma King through empowerment.
Next, one binds the Vajra Song Mudrā;
from the previous mudrā, it gradually ascends from the navel.
Upon reaching their mouths, they dispersed,
producing wondrous and pure sounds to delight the holy assembly.
The mantra is:
Oṃ padmanidhi nidhyāya. By means of this offering of the vajra song, one shall before long possess the eloquence of a Tathāgata.
Next, bind the Vajra Dance mudrā;
visualize clouds of sublime dancers making universal offerings.
With concentration, wisdom, diligence, and power, perform the dance in rotation.
To the left side, the right side, and again over the heart;
with each movement of power, perform three circumambulations.
Without ceasing the recitation of the mantra, scatter [the offerings] above the crown of the head.
Oṃ padmanṛtye kṛta. By means of this offering of sublime dance, one shall obtain the Tathāgata’s mind-born body (manomayakāya).
Next, form the mudrā for the outer offering of burning incense.
By performing this, one universally perfumes the ocean-like assembly of Buddhas.
Join the palms together at the level of the vajra and then scatter them downward.
Visualize clouds of sublime fragrance pervading the entire dharma-realm.
The mantra is:
Oṃ padma-dhūpe svāhā. This is for the purpose of making an offering of incense.
One immediately attains the unimpeded wisdom of the Tathāgata;
universally pervading the world,
one offers sublime incense and obtains the supreme wisdom of all Buddhas.
Next, bind the Vajra Flower-scattering mudrā.
Adorn all world-systems with this;
from the bound mudrā, scatter [the fingers] like flowers.
Fragrant clouds of flowers pervade the entire dharma realm.
The mantra says:
Oṃ padma puṣpe dhūpa-jvala-vajra-puṣpa-pūjāye.
May I swiftly realize the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata,
and may all sentient beings likewise achieve the thirty-two marks of a Buddha.
Next, form the Vajra Lamp Illumination mudrā:
interlace the six fingers of the thumbs and ring fingers externally;
bend the index and middle fingers inward to support each other like the shape of a jewel.
The two fingers of dhyāna and prajñā are each doubled over.
The light of the maṇi-lamp illuminates the dharma-realm.
The secret mantra says:
Oṃ pramāṇi pe. One who performs this rite makes an offering with the lamp of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which enables sentient beings to swiftly accomplish the wisdom of a Tathāgata.
By means of this offering, one attains the purification of the five eyes.
Next, bind the Vajra-unguent mudrā and use it to make offerings to the assembly of all Buddhas.
Releasing the vajra-bind as if scattering fragrant ointments,
the aroma pervades the worlds of the ten directions,
universally perfuming the assembly of noble ones and the śrāvakas.
The mantra is:
Oṃ padmāyatike. When performing this rite, one should wear [the garment] by means of all the Tathāgatas.
They offer the fragrance of wisdom and ethical discipline as an offering,
thereby enabling sentient beings [to attain liberation].
One will swiftly attain purity.
By virtue of this merit, one shall be endowed with the fivefold Dharma-body (pañcāṅga-dharmakāya).
Next, bind the root mudrā.
Next, one should clearly visualize oneself as identical to the deity,
surrounded by the retinue, abiding within the Great Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
Then, with the two hands of concentration and wisdom, perform the vajra-bond (*vajrabandha*).
Erecting the victory banner of the two stages of patience and aspiration,
one recites the root mantra of Avalokiteśvara;
the body abides within a lunar disc, identical to a sattva.
The mantra is:
Oṃ lu-ke śva-ra rāja hṛīḥ. Following this, one should sing various hymns of praise.
When offering praise, at dawn, having washed and sprinkled oneself and anointed the hands, one should form the mudrā and sing the praises with a sublime, elegant, and pure voice.
At the four periods of each day— namely, at dawn, midday, dusk, and midnight—
one should perform the recitation with a rosary according to the respective family (*kula*) of the deity,
followed by the offering of *argha* water.
Next, perform the seal of the three times rotating counter-clockwise to release the boundary seal;
then, immediately bind the Vajra Liberation Seal to bid farewell to all the holy ones.
Next, form the seal for dismissal.
Using the root seal,
move it from the navel up to the face.
Then, dispersing [the visualization],
join the palms above the crown of the head and imagine that the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja returns to his original palace.
Recite the secret mantra:
Oṃ vajrapadma muḥ. Having completed the dismissal of the *iṣṭadevatā*, make aspirations as you wish.
Then, protect the body with the armor mudrā (*kavaca-mudrā*).
Using the boundary-binding mudrā of Hayagrīva,
release the boundary by rotating it counter-clockwise,
and then walk about as you please.
Diligently maintaining incense and flowers,
they recite and chant the Mahāyāna sūtras throughout the four modes of deportment.
Constantly recollect the Honored One without interruption.
If there are sentient beings...
Those who practice this teaching shall realize the Stage of Joy within their present lifetime.
After sixteen lifetimes beyond this, one will attain Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
*Vajraśekhara Sūtra Yoga: The Practice Method of the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja*.
